title: Crowley County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Crowley County well depths run around 40 ft with a 45 gpm median yield. See what that means for drilling cost, water level, and buying rural property.
h1: Water wells in Crowley County, Colorado
intro_html: In Crowley County, most wells are plains wells into shallow sediments and fractured bedrock, not the deep Denver Basin. Records for 1,091 permitted wells give a pretty good picture of how deep you’ll drill, how much water you’re likely to see, and what it tends to cost. If you’re looking at land near Ordway, Sugar City, Olney Springs or Crowley, the numbers below are based on actual permits and well logs in this county.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Crowley County
sections.html:
Crowley County is mostly a shallow drilling area. The median well depth is only about 40 feet, with the middle half of wells between roughly 30 and 70 feet. About 87% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, and only 12% fall between 100 and 300 feet. A very small share, around 1%, go beyond 600 feet, and the deepest well on record hits 2,035 feet, which is an outlier.

For bidding, most drillers here will assume a shallow domestic or stock well in that 30–70 foot band, unless they see reason to plan deeper. Even so, every parcel is different, especially in fractured bedrock, so you still budget for the higher end of that common range.

sections.heading: Well production and how much water to expect
sections.html:
Production in Crowley County is generally strong for such shallow completions. The median reported yield is about 45 gallons per minute, and the middle half of tested wells falls between roughly 10 and 310 gallons per minute. That’s a very wide spread, but it tells you good irrigation and stock wells are common.

On the low side, 8% of reported wells make between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, 25% are in the 5 to 15 gallon per minute band, and about 68% report 15 gallons per minute or better. None of the tested wells report under 1 gallon per minute. For a single home on an exempt household well, anything above a few gallons per minute is usually workable with proper storage.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they show over time
sections.html:
Only 41 Crowley County wells report a static water level, but the pattern is consistent: the median depth to water is around 18 feet, with the middle half between roughly 15 and 23 feet below ground. That’s a fairly shallow water table for the plains, which helps keep total drilling depth down.

Looking over time, the median measured water level was about 16 feet below surface in the 2010s and about 21 feet in the 2020s. That suggests a modest downward trend over the past decade. It’s not dramatic, but it does argue for setting your pump low enough in the hole and leaving some room if levels keep easing down.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and permit history
sections.html:
Crowley County has a long record of well development. Permits show activity in every decade since the 1950s, with 88 permits in the 1950s, 91 in the 1970s, and 97 in the 1990s. Things picked up in the 2000s with 182 permits, then eased to 106 in the 2010s and 31 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit on record is from 2025, so drilling is still active.

Most wells are in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with just a handful tagged as alluvial or Dakota. Drill records name contractors like Authorized (Pe, Pg), Kunau Drilling LLC (Kunau, Timothy R.), and Eastwood Drilling (Eastwood, Francis) among the most active in the county.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Crowley County
sections.html:
Here the ground is mostly alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, so drilling costs stay in a fairly predictable band. Typical rates run around $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone pencils out to roughly $1,400–$2,200.

Once you add steel or PVC casing, grout, a submersible pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house and electrical work, a complete domestic setup at that median depth generally comes in around $7,400–$14,200. If your specific well site requires going deeper than the county median, cost scales up almost directly with depth at that same per-foot rate.

sections.heading: Local risks: water quality, low yield, and siting
sections.html:
On the yield side, the Crowley County data are encouraging: none of the tested wells report less than 1 gallon per minute, and a large share do better than 15 gallons per minute. Still, single-well data are sparse, so a dry or weak hole is always a possibility, especially in fractured bedrock.

For water quality, state and federal maps show several potential concern areas here: 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles in the county. That doesn’t mean your well is contaminated, but it does mean you should plan on a full lab test panel when a new well is drilled or when buying a property.

sections.heading: Buying or building on land in Crowley County
sections.html:
When you’re evaluating a tract around Ordway, Sugar City, Olney Springs or Crowley, start by pulling nearby well permits to see actual depths and yields, not just the county medians. With a 40-foot median depth and shallow water levels around 18 feet, a typical domestic or stock well should be straightforward, but the spread in yields means you still want to see local data.

Confirm your intended use lines up with the permit type: roughly 35% of existing wells are domestic or household, 47% are stock, 24% irrigation and 9% monitoring. Make sure septic setbacks, building location and well location all fit on the parcel before you close, so you’re not boxed in later by separation requirements.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Crowley County, Colorado?
faq.a: Well records in Crowley County show a median depth of about 40 feet, with the middle half of wells between roughly 30 and 70 feet deep. About 87% of wells are under 100 feet, and only about 12% are in the 100–300 foot range. A very small fraction extend much deeper, including one well recorded at 2,035 feet, but those are exceptions, not the norm.

faq.q: How much water do Crowley County wells typically produce?
faq.a: Reported production is generally strong. The median yield among tested wells is about 45 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs between roughly 10 and 310 gallons per minute. Around 8% of wells fall in the 1–5 gallon per minute range, 25% are between 5 and 15, and about 68% report 15 gallons per minute or more. None of the tested wells report under 1 gallon per minute.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Crowley County, CO?
faq.a: With alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, typical drilling rates run about $35–$55 per foot in Crowley County. At the county’s 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone might run roughly $1,400–$2,200. A complete domestic well with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical commonly totals about $7,400–$14,200 at that depth, with cost increasing as you drill deeper.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Crowley County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well. Crowley County has 5 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, so testing is important. A new or existing well should be checked with a full lab analysis for bacteria, nitrates, basic chemistry and, where appropriate, PFAS or metals, then treated if needed based on results.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping in Crowley County?
faq.a: Limited static water level data suggest a modest decline. The median measured water level was about 16 feet below ground surface in the 2010s and about 21 feet in the 2020s. Overall, current measurements show a median depth to water around 18 feet, with the middle half between about 15 and 23 feet. When designing a new well, it’s smart to set the pump low enough to allow for some further drawdown.
